content: Bacterial vaginosis (BV) is a common vaginal infection, with a global prevalence ranging from 10% to 50%. It is characterized by an imbalance in the normal vaginal microbiota. Microorganisms associated with BV have also been identified in the male genital tract, and their presence may contribute to the recurrence of BV in women following antibiotic treatment. Consequently, treating the sexual partners of women with BV has been proposed as a strategy to reduce recurrence rates and the overall burden of the disease. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of concurrent antibiotic treatment for the sexual partners of women with BV in improving clinical and symptomatic outcomes in women, as well as to assess the safety of such treatment in men. A comprehensive search of multiple databases and registries was conducted up to July 23, 2016, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the Web of Science. Additional sources, such as conference proceedings and reference lists of relevant studies, were also reviewed. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing antibiotic treatment for sexual partners with placebo, no intervention, or other interventions were included. Seven RCTs involving a total of 1026 participants met the inclusion criteria. Four of these trials were funded by the pharmaceutical industry. Five trials (854 participants) compared antibiotic treatment for sexual partners with placebo. High-quality evidence demonstrated that antibiotic treatment did not improve clinical or symptomatic outcomes in women during the first week (risk ratio [RR] 0.99, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.96 to 1.03; 712 participants, four studies; RR 1.06, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.12; 577 participants, three studies, respectively), between the first and fourth week (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.11; 590 participants, three studies; RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.03; 444 participants, two studies, respectively), or after the fourth week (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.07; 572 participants, four studies; RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.17; 296 participants, two studies, respectively). Antibiotic treatment did not reduce the recurrence of BV during the first and fourth week (RR 1.28, 95% CI 0.68 to 2.43; 218 participants, one study; low-quality evidence) or after the fourth week (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.52; 372 participants, three studies; low-quality evidence). However, it was associated with an increased frequency of adverse events, primarily gastrointestinal symptoms, reported by sexual partners (RR 2.55, 95% CI 1.55 to 4.18; 477 participants, three studies; low-quality evidence). Two trials (172 participants) compared antibiotic treatment for sexual partners with no intervention. When compared with no intervention, the effects of antibiotic treatment on recurrence rates after the fourth week (RR 1.71, 95% CI 0.65 to 4.55; 51 participants, one study), clinical improvement between the first and fourth week (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.25; 152 participants, two studies), and symptomatic improvement after the fourth week (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.39 to 1.11; 70 participants, one study) were inconclusive, with no significant differences observed between groups. The quality of evidence for these outcomes was downgraded to low or very low. In conclusion, high-quality evidence indicates that antibiotic treatment for the sexual partners of women with BV does not improve clinical or symptomatic outcomes in women during the first week, between the first and fourth week, or after the fourth week when compared with placebo. Low-quality evidence suggests that such treatment does not reduce recurrence rates during the first and fourth week or after the fourth week but does increase the frequency of adverse events in sexual partners. Finally, when compared with no intervention, antibiotic treatment does not reduce recurrence rates after the fourth week or improve clinical or symptomatic outcomes in women during the first and fourth week or after the fourth week.
